props.title: Le Deuxième Souffle

sections.content: Jean-Pierre Melville's Le Deuxième Souffle (1966) stands as a masterclass in French crime cinema, bridging the gap between classic film noir and the emerging New Wave. Melville's meticulous attention to detail and stripped-down style influenced countless crime films that followed. The film's protagonist Gu, played with stoic intensity by Lino Ventura, exemplifies the director's fascination with honor among thieves - a theme he would perfect in later works like Le Samouraï (1967) and Le Cercle Rouge (1970).

sections.content: The film's legendary 20-minute heist sequence, shot with documentary-like precision, influenced later directors like Michael Mann in Heat (1995) and Christopher Nolan in Inception (2010). Melville's stark visual style, with its emphasis on procedure and process over dialogue, created a template for the modern crime thriller. The existential weight carried by criminal protagonists in films like Drive (2011) and The American (2010) can be traced directly back to Melville's work. SUBHEAD: The Melville Touch: Style and Influence

What sets Le Deuxième Souffle apart is its brutal efficiency in storytelling. The film strips away melodrama to focus on pure cinema - gesture, movement, and precisely composed frames. This approach influenced the French polar (crime film) genre and international directors like John Woo, who cited Melville as a major influence on films like The Killer (1989). The movie's exploration of loyalty and betrayal among criminals became a blueprint for contemporary crime dramas like The Departed (2006) and Layer Cake (2004).
